questions.prompt: Which update does **Levenberg-Marquardt** compute, and what happens when the new cost is *higher* than the old one?
options: $(J^\top J)\Delta = -J^\top r$; always accept the step
$(J^\top J + \lambda I)\Delta = -J^\top r$; accept the step and decrease $\lambda$
$(J^\top J + \lambda I)\Delta = -J^\top r$; reject the step and increase $\lambda$ (e.g. ×10)
$\Delta = -\lambda J^\top r$; halve the step
questions.explanation: LM damps the GN system. With large $\lambda$ the step becomes $\approx -b/\lambda$, a short gradient-descent step. With small $\lambda$ it is the GN step. A failed step is **rejected** (the state is kept) and $\lambda$ grows; a successful one is accepted and $\lambda$ shrinks (÷10). Plain GN has no such safeguard and can diverge from a poor initial guess or with large residuals.

questions.prompt: In a pose graph, what does the information matrix $\Omega_{ij}$ of an edge represent?
options: The inverse of the measurement covariance: how much we trust each residual component
The Jacobian of the edge residual
The covariance of the measurement
The Hessian of the full problem
questions.explanation: $\Omega = \Sigma^{-1}$, so the cost is $e^\top\Omega e$, the squared Mahalanobis distance. A precise measurement (small $\Sigma$) gets a large weight. After solving, $H = \sum J^\top\Omega J$ approximates the inverse covariance of the *estimate*, which is where marginal covariances come from.

questions.prompt: Why does the bundle-adjustment Hessian have a block-sparse **arrow** structure?
options: Because cameras are ordered by timestamp
Because the Jacobian is dense
Because of the Schur complement
Each reprojection residual depends on exactly one camera and one landmark, so camera–camera and landmark–landmark off-diagonal blocks are zero
questions.explanation: A residual $r_{ij}$ touches only camera $i$ and point $j$. So $H_{cc}$ is block-diagonal (6×6 blocks), $H_{pp}$ is block-diagonal (3×3 blocks), and only $H_{cp}$ couples them. Ordering points after cameras gives the arrow shape, which is exactly what makes the Schur complement on the points cheap.

questions.prompt: You run Gauss-Newton on a 2D pose graph without fixing any pose. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; GN finds the unique solution
$H$ is singular: the cost is invariant to a global SE(2) transform (3-dim gauge freedom), so the linear solve is ill-posed
The residuals become non-differentiable
The loop closure is ignored
questions.explanation: Relative-pose residuals do not change if every pose is moved by the same rigid transform, so $H$ has a 3-dimensional null space (6 in SE(3), 7 in monocular sim(3)). Fix $x_0$ by removing its block or adding a strong prior such as $10^6 I$ on $H_{00}$. A tiny LM damping would also make it solvable, but the solution would drift.

questions.prompt: Your numerical Jacobian uses **forward** differences $(f(x+\epsilon)-f(x))/\epsilon$ with $\epsilon = 10^{-12}$. The analytic and numerical Jacobians disagree at the 1e-4 level. The most likely cause?
options: The analytic Jacobian is wrong
Forward differences are exact for linear functions
$\epsilon$ is too small: floating-point cancellation dominates. Use central differences with $\epsilon \approx 10^{-6}$
Eigen's default precision is float
questions.explanation: There are two error sources. Truncation is $O(\epsilon)$ for forward differences and $O(\epsilon^2)$ for central ones. Round-off is $\approx \epsilon_{mach}|f|/\epsilon$. With $\epsilon=10^{-12}$ the round-off is about $10^{-4}$. Central differences with $\epsilon\approx 10^{-6}$ balance the two at roughly $10^{-10}$.

questions.prompt: With **Huber** weights (threshold $k$), what is the IRLS weight of a residual $r = 4k$?
questions.explanation: $w(r) = 1$ for $|r|\le k$, else $k/|r| = 1/4$. That turns the quadratic cost into a linear one for large residuals, so an outlier's *influence* $w\,r = k\,\mathrm{sign}(r)$ is bounded. Cauchy goes further, $w = 1/(1+(r/c)^2)$, and down-weights outliers towards 0. The threshold applies to the whitened residual.

questions.prompt: Marginalising state block $c$ from $\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\B^\top&C\end{bmatrix}\Delta = \begin{bmatrix}b_a\\b_c\end{bmatrix}$ gives which reduced system?
options: $(A - B^\top C^{-1} B)\Delta_a = b_a - B^\top C^{-1} b_c$
$A\Delta_a = b_a$
$(A + B C^{-1} B^\top)\Delta_a = b_a + B C^{-1} b_c$
$(A - B C^{-1} B^\top)\Delta_a = b_a - B C^{-1} b_c$
questions.explanation: Take the second row, $\Delta_c = C^{-1}(b_c - B^\top\Delta_a)$, and substitute it into the first. Dimensions check: $B$ is $n_a\times n_c$, so $BC^{-1}B^\top$ is $n_a\times n_a$. The result is generally **dense**, which is the fill-in that makes sliding-window VIO priors dense. Because the linearisation point gets frozen, FEJ is used to keep the system consistent.

questions.prompt: **IMU preintegration** (Forster et al.). Why integrate IMU measurements between keyframes into relative $\Delta R, \Delta v, \Delta p$ instead of integrating in the world frame?
options: It removes the need for gravity
The relative terms do not depend on the start pose/velocity, so changing those during optimisation needs no re-integration; bias changes are handled by first-order Jacobians
It makes the IMU noise zero
World-frame integration is impossible in floating point
questions.explanation: World-frame integration starts from $R_i, v_i, p_i$. Each time the optimiser moves those, you would have to re-integrate hundreds of samples. Preintegrated deltas are expressed in frame $i$, with gravity pulled out, so they are constants of the factor. A small bias update is applied as $\Delta R(b) \approx \Delta R(\bar b)\,\mathrm{Exp}(J_b\,\delta b)$ rather than by re-integrating.
